kernelIdea: S ∪ T holds anything in at least one; S ∩ T holds things in both. S ⊆ S∪T and S∩T ⊆ S always. Disjoint means empty intersection.

kernels.l1: The overlap holds what is in both hoops. Everything in either hoop, all together, is the big pile.
kernels.l2: Put two hoops on the floor. The overlap is the things in both hoops. Everything in either hoop, counted once, is the whole collection. If the hoops never overlap, nothing is in both.
kernels.l3: The union of two collections holds everything in either one; the overlap holds everything in both. Union goes with *or*, overlap goes with *and*.
kernels.l4: The union of two sets holds everything in either; their intersection holds everything in both. Union is *or* and intersection is *and*. Sets with nothing in common are called disjoint.
kernels.l5: Union and intersection are the set-level versions of *or* and *and*. The intersection sits inside each set, and each set sits inside the union.
kernels.l6: Union collects what lies in at least one of the sets, intersection what lies in both — the set versions of *or* and *and*. The intersection is always inside each set, and each set is always inside the union.
kernels.l7: Union and intersection are defined by *or* and *and* on membership conditions. The intersection always sits inside each set and each sits inside the union; disjoint means the intersection is empty.
kernels.l8: Union collects what is in at least one; intersection collects what is in all. Both extend from two sets to a whole family, where *at least one* and *all* become §1.10's two quantifier words.
